title: SLO Shadowing and Capacity Canary Framework
author: Evelyn Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose
This page documents the SLO Shadowing and Capacity Canary Framework: a lightweight, repeatable pattern SREs and service owners can use to validate SLO behavior, verify capacity plans, and exercise graceful-degradation paths before wide rollouts. The framework bridges correctness (SLO observability) and capacity safety (canarying load on a controlled pool).

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference services and multi-tenant routing layers (hosted API, Dedicated pools).
- Primary focus: production-similar traffic replay, progressive capacity ramping, and SLO metric shadow evaluation.
- Not intended for full security/compliance certification or long-term load testing (use dedicated performance harness).

Key principles
- Shadow, don’t disturb: shadowed SLO evaluation must not affect real traffic paths or budgets.
- Small, measurable steps: ramp canaries using discrete capacity increments (5% -> 20% -> 50%).
- Observability-first: each canary must have a dashboard and pre-defined stop/rollback criteria.
- Actionable alerts: SLO guardrails convert directly to runbook steps.

Terminology
- Shadow SLO: running the SLO evaluation logic in parallel against a mirrored stream of requests to measure expected behavior without influencing live routing decisions.
- Capacity Canary: a controlled experiment that routes a proportion of real or synthetic traffic to a target deployment to validate capacity behavior.
- Capacity Bridge: temporary autoscale and routing configuration applied during canaries to ensure controlled resource allocation.

Architecture (textual diagram)
1) Traffic Replay / Traffic Forker -> 2) Shadow Evaluator (stateless service) \u2014> metrics (SLO success, latency P50/P95/P99, token cost) 
                                           
                                          +-> 3) Canary Pool (isolated nodes) -> realtime metrics (GPU utilisation, queue length)

Components and responsibilities
- Traffic Forker: duplicates a sample of incoming production requests to the shadow stream. Responsible: service owner.
- Shadow Evaluator: computes SLO checks (latency, error classification, output sanity). Responsible: eng-platform / observability.
- Canary Orchestrator: applies Capacity Bridge, controls percentage routing, and records experiment metadata (owner, start/stop, commit). Responsible: eng-sre.
- Metric Collector / Analyzer: composite dashboards and automated stop triggers. Responsible: observability team.

SLOs evaluated in shadowing
- Latency SLO: p95 < 1200ms for short-text generation routes; p99 < 2500ms for long contexts.
- Correctness SLO (syntactic): 99.5% pass rate on structural output checks (valid JSON, schema conformance).
- Error SLO: < 0.5% 5xx rate across evaluated routes.
- Cost guardrail: 95th token-cost-per-request must not exceed baseline by > 25% during canary.

Pre-run checklist (must be green before starting)
1) Owner and experiment name recorded in the Canary Orchestrator.
2) Observability dashboards instantiated with baseline comparisons.
3) Canary pool capacity allocated (minimum 3 nodes for redundancy).
4) Alerting hooks configured: stop/rollback thresholds for each SLO metric.
5) Synthetic traffic blocks validated and alignment with sampled production traffic verified.

Canary run procedure (step-by-step)
1) Initialize: tag experiment and capture baseline metrics (last 24h).
2) Shadow-only validation (0% real routing): run shadow evaluator on real-time fork; verify SLO differences <= 2x acceptable drift.
3) Synthetic soak (5% equivalent load): use replay generator to apply 5% of peak qps to canary pool with Capacity Bridge protections in place. Observe for 30 minutes.
4) Progressive ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% (30-minute holds or until steady-state). At each step evaluate:
   - latency p95/p99 delta vs baseline
   - error rate and error classification (model timeout, OOM, networking)
   - queue length and GPU util
   - cost per token delta
5) Stop/rollback criteria (automatic):
   - latency p99 > baseline p99 * 2 for two consecutive windows (5m)
   - 5xx rate > 1% sustained for 10m
   - GPU queue length > 2x steady baseline or OOMs observed
   - cost-per-token exceeds guardrail for 3 consecutive evaluation windows
6) If all checks pass at 50% hold, schedule full rollout gating (hand-off to deployment and product QA).

Incident and post-failure runbook (short)
- If automated rollback triggers:
  1) Canary Orchestrator drains canary pool and re-routes traffic back to baseline nodes.
  2) SRE runbook: collect trace slices for failed window, capture kernel/scheduler logs, dump KV cache metrics.
  3) Annotate experiment with failure reason tags (latency, OOM, model-regression).
  4) Open a triage issue in the SLO regression board and assign to owner.

Data and metrics to collect
- request_id, route, tenant_id (hashed for privacy), request_size_tokens, response_tokens, model_variant, backend_node, start_ts, end_ts, result_code, error_class
- resource metrics: gpu_util_pct, gpu_mem_used_mb, preemption_events, queue_depth, docker_restart_count
- derived SLO metrics: success_rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, token_cost_per_request

Example stop-condition PromQL snippets (examples for observability team)
- p99 latency spike (5m rolling):
  avg_over_time(service_latency_p99[5m]) > (baseline_p99 * 2)
- elevated 5xx rate (10m):
  increase(http_server_errors_total{code~"5.."}[10m]) / increase(http_requests_total[10m]) > 0.01

Safety engineering: Capacity Bridge configuration (sample table)
| config_key | recommended_value | rationale |
|-----------|-------------------:|----------|
| min_nodes | "3" | maintain redundancy during canary |
| reserve_cpu_pct | "20" | headroom for autoscaler spikes |
| reserve_gpu_mem_mb | "1024" | avoid OOM boundary conditions |
| probe_interval_s | "30" | quick detection of regressions |

Ownership and governance
- Canary orchestration owner: eng-sre / capacity-sig.
- Shadow evaluator maintenance: observability team.
- Service owners must sign off on final rollouts and confirm acceptable correctness thresholds.
- Quarterly review: every team runs at least one SLO shadow + capacity canary for high-impact routes.

Operational tooling snippets
- Start a named canary with the orchestrator CLI:
  rdo canary start --name "chatv2-slo-shadow-2026-01" --service "chatv2" --pool "canary-gpu-n1" --ramp "5,20,50" --hold-min 30
- Query shadowed SLO output (example JSON):
  {
    \"experiment\": \"chatv2-slo-shadow-2026-01\",
    \"p95_latency_ms\": \"890\",
    \"p99_latency_ms\": \"1320\",
    \"error_rate\": \"0.21%\"
  }

Rollout gating checklist (pre-decision)
- Shadow SLO drift within expected bounds (owner confirmation).
- Canary pool metrics stable for one canary hold period.
- Cost impact acceptable to finance guardrail.
- Post-canary signoff: service owner + eng-sre + observability.

Postmortem template for canary failures (condensed)
- Title, experiment id, owner, start/stop times
- Observed symptoms and metric deltas (attach dashboard snapshots)
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (kernel logs, model regression diffs)
- Action items (short/medium/long-term) with owners and ETA
- Test plan to validate fix (including shadow re-run)

Appendix: small examples and heuristics
- Use a hashed tenant_id when collecting telemetry for customer-sensitive services.
- For models with long runtimes (>= 10s), length-aware SLO windows (p95 over 1h) are recommended.
- If canary detects model quality regressions, run A/B evaluation harness against curated prompt set before any scaling decisions.
